The move is expected to have significant implications for both Manchester City and Barcelona, as they navigate the upcoming season with their respective squads.

The transfer of Kerolin to Barcelona marks a significant development in the women's football landscape, with the WSL continuing to attract top talent from around the world. As the new season approaches, fans will be watching with interest to see how Manchester City adapts to the loss of their star forward, and how Kerolin fares in her new role at Barcelona. With the transfer now officially confirmed, attention will turn to the upcoming fixtures and the impact of this deal on the teams involved.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Marlen Reusser Maintains Tour de France Femmes Lead
content:
In a thrilling display of skill and determination, Mauritian rider Kim Le Court has secured her second Tour de France Femmes stage win, outsprinting French rider Cédrine Kerbaol and Queen of the Mountains classification leader Puck Pieterse in Tournon-sur-Rhone. This victory marks a significant milestone for Le Court, who overcame a mechanical issue earlier in the stage to join the day's breakaway group and ultimately claim the top spot on the podium.

The stage, which took place in central France, was characterized by scorching temperatures, making the ride even more challenging for the competitors. Despite these conditions, Le Court persevered and managed to recover from her mechanical problem on the climb of the Col de Lalouvesc. Her ability to bounce back and join the breakaway group ultimately paid off, as she was able to outmaneuver her rivals in the final sprint. Meanwhile, Marlen Reusser retained her overall lead in the Tour de France Femmes, fending off a strong challenge from rival Demi Vollering.

The win is a testament to Le Court's skill and perseverance, and she was understandably elated by her achievement. As she reflected on her victory, she noted that "winning a stage in a Tour de France is very special," highlighting the significance of this accomplishment in her career. With this win, Le Court has cemented her place in the history of the Tour de France Femmes, and her performance will undoubtedly be remembered as one of the highlights of the competition.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Springboks and All Blacks Launch Greatest Rivalry Tour
content:
The highly anticipated Rugby's Greatest Rivalry (RGR) series between South Africa and New Zealand is set to kick off, bringing with it a wave of nostalgia and excitement for fans of the sport. The series, billed as a "tour like no other", promises to be an intense and thrilling competition between two of rugby's greatest teams. To mark the occasion, the Springboks have unveiled a special edition jersey that will be worn only four times before being retired, adding to the sense of exclusivity and uniqueness surrounding the event.

However, despite the focus on the on-field action, the series is also being overshadowed by a looming legal battle in South Africa. The dispute centers on the commercial identity of the series and the unauthorized use of its branding, highlighting the complex and often contentious world of sports marketing. This development serves as a reminder that, even in the romanticized world of sports, commercial considerations and legal issues can often take center stage. As the series gets underway, fans will be watching with bated breath to see how the action unfolds, both on and off the field.

The RGR series is poised to be a thrilling and closely contested competition, with both teams eager to prove their mettle and claim bragging rights. As the Springboks take to the field in their special edition jerseys, fans will be hoping that the focus can remain on the rugby, rather than the off-field distractions. With the series promising to be an unforgettable experience for fans, it remains to be seen how the legal battle will play out and what impact it will have on the overall spectacle.
author: Guardian Sport

title: London Spirit Eliminated from Men's Hundred
content:
London Spirit became the first team eliminated from the men's Hundred competition after a six‑wicket loss to MI London at Lord’s. The match, played on a pitch that favored the bowlers, saw MI London secure victory with 14 overs to spare, leaving Spirit unable to reach the target of 148 runs.

MI London’s bowlers exploited early swings, taking four wickets in the opening overs and maintaining pressure throughout the innings. Spirit’s batting lineup struggled to establish partnerships, and a crucial collapse in the middle overs left them chasing a difficult total. The result has confirmed MI London’s place in the semi‑finals, while Spirit’s campaign ends abruptly.

With the tournament progressing, MI London will now prepare to face the next opponent in the knockout stage, while the other teams will vie for the remaining semi‑final spots. The early exit underscores the competitive nature of the Hundred, where a single match can determine a team’s fate.
author: BBC Sport

title: Rangers Lose Europa League Qualifier
content:
Rangers' manager Derek McInnes has reflected on the team's disappointing performance in the Europa League qualifying first-leg match against Jagiellonia Bialystok in Poland. The Scottish side suffered a defeat, and McInnes attributed the loss to the team's own mistakes, stating that they were "guilty of beating ourselves." This admission suggests that the manager believes his team had the capability to secure a better outcome, but ultimately fell short due to self-inflicted errors.

The match saw Rangers concede cheap goals, which McInnes identified as a key factor in the defeat. The loss of these goals not only affected the scoreline but also impacted the team's overall performance and morale. McInnes' comments imply that the mistakes made by his team were avoidable and that they had the potential to achieve a more favorable result if they had been more vigilant and composed in defense. The first-leg defeat puts Rangers at a disadvantage ahead of the second leg, and McInnes will likely be working with his team to address the issues that led to the loss and to devise a strategy to overturn the deficit.

The Europa League qualifying campaign is a crucial one for Rangers, and the team will need to regroup and refocus ahead of the second leg. McInnes' assessment of the first-leg defeat highlights the importance of minimizing errors and being more resilient in defense. With the second leg looming, Rangers will be seeking to learn from their mistakes and produce a stronger performance to keep their European ambitions alive.
author: BBC Sport

title: Wigan Warriors beat St Helens in Super Four opener
content:
The Wigan Warriors have made a strong statement in the inaugural match of the new Super Four format of the Women's Super League, defeating St Helens 44-6. This opening match sets the tone for the revamped competition, which promises to bring a new level of intensity and excitement to the women's rugby league scene. The Super Four format is designed to pit the top teams against each other in a condensed and highly competitive schedule, and Wigan's dominant performance suggests they are well-equipped to navigate this challenging new landscape.

The match itself was a one-sided affair, with Wigan's attacking prowess proving too much for St Helens to handle. The Warriors' backline was particularly impressive, with their speed and agility allowing them to exploit gaps in the St Helens defense and score a string of tries. The 44-6 scoreline is a testament to Wigan's clinical finishing and their ability to capitalize on scoring opportunities. St Helens, on the other hand, will be looking to regroup and reassess their strategy after a tough opening loss. Despite the setback, they will be eager to bounce back and prove themselves in the remaining matches of the Super Four.

The convincing win for Wigan Warriors has established them as early favorites in the Super Four competition, and their performance will be closely watched by fans and rivals alike. As the Women's Super League continues to grow and gain momentum, matches like this one will be crucial in shaping the narrative of the season. With Wigan setting the bar high, the other teams in the Super Four will need to raise their game if they hope to challenge the Warriors for the top spot.
author: BBC Sport

title: Manchester City Winger Signs New Contract
content:
Manchester City has secured the long-term commitment of winger Jeremy Doku, with the player signing a new contract that will keep him at the club until 2031. This move is the latest in a series of contract extensions for key players at Manchester City, as the club continues to build a strong foundation for future success. By tying down Doku to a lengthy deal, Manchester City is ensuring that the talented young winger will remain a key part of the team's plans for years to come.

The new contract is a significant development for both Doku and Manchester City, as it demonstrates the club's faith in the player's abilities and provides him with the stability and security to focus on his development. Doku has already shown promise in his time at Manchester City, and the club will be hoping that he can continue to grow and improve as a player. With this new contract in place, Doku will have the opportunity to establish himself as a key player for Manchester City and contribute to the club's pursuit of success in domestic and international competitions.

The signing of Doku's new contract is a positive move for Manchester City, as it helps to maintain a sense of continuity and stability within the squad. With Doku committed to the club until 2031, Manchester City can now look to the future with confidence, knowing that one of its most talented young players is set to remain a key part of the team for years to come. This contract extension is a significant piece of business for the club, and it will be interesting to see how Doku develops and contributes to Manchester City's success in the years ahead.
author: BBC Sport

title: Vinicius Jr Signs New Real Madrid Contract
content:
Real Madrid winger Vinicius Jr has secured his future at the club after agreeing to improved contract terms, bringing an end to speculation linking him with a transfer to Arsenal. The Brazilian international will remain at the Santiago Bernabéu, confirming his commitment to the Spanish side following successful negotiations that addressed his contractual demands.

The agreement resolves a period of
author: BBC Sport

title: Teamsters Sue California Over Self-Driving Truck Rules
content:
The International Brotherhood of Teamsters, a labor union representing truck drivers and other transportation workers in California, has filed a lawsuit against the state's Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) and other agencies. The lawsuit, which was filed in Alameda County on Wednesday, centers on the approval of self-driving trucks for operation on California's roads. According to the Teamsters, state officials failed to conduct a thorough economic study and analysis of the practical impact of allowing autonomous trucks to operate in the state, as required by law.

The lawsuit alleges that the California DMV and other agencies did not follow the necessary procedures when approving the deployment of self-driving trucks, potentially putting the livelihoods of human truck drivers at risk. Attorneys for the Teamsters argue that the state's failure to complete the required economic study and impact analysis means that the approval of autonomous trucks was not done in accordance with the law. The Teamsters are seeking to ensure that the state follows the proper procedures and considers the potential effects on truck drivers and other workers in the transportation industry.

The outcome of the lawsuit could have significant implications for the development and deployment of autonomous trucking technology in California. If the court rules in favor of the Teamsters, it could lead to a re-evaluation of the state's approach to regulating self-driving trucks and potentially slow the rollout of this technology. The case highlights the ongoing debate over the impact of automation on workers in various industries, including transportation, and the need for careful consideration of the economic and social implications of emerging technologies.
author: The Hill

title: Virginia Governor Spanberger to intervene in NextEra-Dominion merger
content:
Virginia Governor Abigail Spanberger (D) announced Thursday that she intends to intervene in the pending merger between NextEra Energy and Dominion Energy, which, if approved, would create the largest regulated electrical utility in the world. In an op‑ed published in the Washington Post, Spanberger explained that she will make herself a party to the transaction and will seek to influence the regulatory review process.

Spanberger’s intervention follows concerns that the combined entity could wield significant market power in the region and potentially impact rates and service reliability for consumers. By joining the merger as a party, she aims to bring a state‑level perspective to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s assessment, ensuring that Virginia’s interests are considered in any approval or conditions that may be imposed.

The governor’s move underscores the growing scrutiny of large utility consolidations and highlights the role state officials can play in shaping outcomes that affect local markets. Her participation may prompt a more thorough examination of the merger’s implications for ratepayers and competition before a final decision is reached.
author: The Hill

title: Trump Arch Proposal Faces Opposition
content:
The National Park Service (NPS) has warned that President Donald Trump’s proposed arch at Memorial Circle would encroach on dozens of historic and cultural sites in Washington, D.C.  The arch, intended to honor the former president, would be positioned on a prominent stretch of the National Mall, but the NPS notes that its footprint would overlap with several federally protected landmarks, including the National World War II Memorial, the Washington Monument’s adjacent plaza, and the surrounding National Mall landscape.  The agency has expressed concern that the structure’s design and placement could compromise the integrity of these sites and disrupt the visual and historical context that the Mall is intended to preserve.

Despite these concerns, the NPS reports that there has been little public discussion of alternative locations for the arch.  The proposal, which has been floated by Trump’s supporters, has not yet undergone a formal environmental review or received input from the broader planning community.  As the project moves forward, the NPS will likely continue to monitor the proposal’s compliance with federal historic preservation statutes and the National Mall’s master plan, while urging stakeholders to consider sites that would not compromise the integrity of the existing memorials and public spaces.
author: NPR Politics

title: Trump Signs Two Immigration Actions to Limit Birthright Citizenship and Curb Birth Tourism
content:
Former President Donald J. Trump recently asserted that his most recent actions were constitutionally sound, according to a statement released by his spokesperson.  The remarks were made during a brief press briefing in which no additional specifics about the actions were disclosed.  Trump’s spokesperson emphasized that the former president believes the measures align with constitutional principles, but no further explanation was offered.

The lack of detail has left analysts and lawmakers uncertain about the nature of the actions in question.  Some observers note that Trump has previously defended a range of initiatives— from executive orders to public statements—by citing constitutional authority.  Without additional information, it is unclear whether the current claim refers to a new policy proposal, a legal challenge, or another form of political activity.

In the absence of further context, the statement remains a general assertion of constitutional compliance.  The former president’s confidence in the legality of his actions is noted, but the lack of detail means the public and officials must await more concrete information before assessing the claim’s implications.
author: NPR Politics

title: Conservatives Propose Ban on Foreign Nationals in Social Housing
content:
The government’s latest housing strategy claims that restricting entitlement to social housing could free up roughly 230,000 homes across the country. The plan, presented by the ruling party, argues that by tightening eligibility criteria and encouraging voluntary relocation, a significant number of properties currently held for social use would become available for private developers and market‑based buyers.

Supporters say the move would increase the supply of affordable homes for the private sector and stimulate construction activity, while critics warn that the policy could leave vulnerable populations without secure accommodation. The proposal is set to be debated in Parliament next month, with stakeholders from housing charities and local councils already calling for a more nuanced approach to safeguarding those most in need.
author: BBC Politics

title: Proteins Help Organs Adapt Circadian Clock
content:
Researchers at Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU) have revealed how the body’s shared circadian clock is fine‑tuned by individual organs to meet their specific physiological demands throughout the day. By combining transcriptomic profiling, proteomics, and functional assays in mouse models, the team showed that while the core clock machinery—comprising transcription factors such as CLOCK, BMAL1, PER, and CRY—operates uniformly across tissues, downstream regulatory networks diverge sharply between organs. This divergence allows each tissue to time processes such as glucose metabolism, immune surveillance, and hormone secretion in a manner that best suits its functional role.

The study identified organ‑specific transcription factors and epigenetic modifications that modulate the output of the core clock, creating distinct rhythmic patterns of gene expression. For example, the liver’s metabolic genes peak in the early morning, whereas the heart’s contractile genes peak later in the day, reflecting the differing metabolic and mechanical demands of each organ. The researchers also demonstrated that disrupting these organ‑specific adaptations in mice leads to metabolic imbalances and impaired cardiac function, underscoring the physiological importance of this tailored timing.

These findings deepen our understanding of circadian biology and highlight the potential for targeted chronotherapeutic strategies. By recognizing that each organ interprets the same internal timekeeping signal in a unique way, future research may develop interventions that align drug delivery or lifestyle modifications with the optimal timing for specific tissues, potentially improving treatment efficacy for metabolic and cardiovascular disorders.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Night Shift Work Linked to Higher Long COVID Risk
content:
A new study has provided the first evidence that night work and chronic insomnia may raise the likelihood of developing long COVID. Researchers report that individuals who regularly work overnight shifts or suffer from persistent sleep disorders experience a higher incidence of prolonged post‑viral symptoms following SARS‑CoV‑2 infection.

The research, led by ISGlobal and supported by the la Caixa Foundation, was conducted in partnership with the Germans Trias i Pujol Research Institute (IGTP) using data from the GCAT | Genomes for Life cohort. The cohort includes thousands of participants whose occupational histories and sleep patterns were linked to their COVID‑19 outcomes. Statistical analysis revealed that night‑shift workers and those with chronic insomnia had a significantly greater risk of reporting long‑COVID symptoms compared with daytime workers and individuals with normal sleep.

These findings underscore the need for targeted preventive measures for vulnerable worker groups and suggest that sleep health may play a critical role in post‑COVID recovery. Further studies are required to confirm the mechanisms underlying this association and to inform public health strategies aimed at reducing long‑COVID morbidity.
author: Medical Xpress

title: FDA Approves Orzeyful, First Narcolepsy Type 1 Drug
content:
The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved Orzeyful (oveporexton) tablets on Thursday for the treatment of narcolepsy type 1 in adults. The new drug is the first medication authorized to address the full spectrum of symptoms associated with this condition, including excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy, and disrupted nighttime sleep.

Orzeyful represents a breakthrough because it directly targets the underlying loss of orexin signaling that causes narcolepsy type 1. By restoring this critical neuropeptide pathway, the drug offers a mechanism‑based approach rather than merely managing individual symptoms. The approval follows clinical trials demonstrating significant improvements in wakefulness and reductions in cataplexy episodes compared with placebo.

The availability of Orzeyful may change the therapeutic landscape for narcolepsy type 1, providing patients with a first‑in‑class option that addresses the root cause of the disease. Further post‑marketing studies will monitor long‑term safety and effectiveness as the medication enters broader clinical use.
author: Medical Xpress

title: E-scooter riders face higher brain injury risk
content:
A study published in *Scientific Reports* reveals that e-scooter riders in England and Wales face a heightened risk of brain and internal organ injuries compared to motorcyclists and cyclists. The research identifies a significant disparity in injury profiles, suggesting that e-scooter users may be more vulnerable to severe trauma than operators of other common transportation modes.

In response to these findings, the authors recommend a comprehensive strategy to improve rider safety,
author: Medical Xpress

title: Immune-Inspired Strategy Enhances Disease Surveillance
content:
A study conducted by researchers from the Perelman School of Medicine at the University of Pennsylvania and the Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia has shown that a disease‑surveillance system modeled on the human immune system can identify more disease‑carrying insects than conventional top‑down methods. The immune‑inspired approach uses distributed, sensor‑based monitoring that mimics how antibodies detect pathogens, allowing for real‑time detection of vectors such as mosquitoes and other insects that transmit diseases like malaria, dengue and Zika.

In the field trials carried out in Peru, the immune‑model system detected a higher density of infected insects across diverse ecological zones compared with standard surveillance protocols that rely on periodic sampling and manual identification. The researchers argue that the decentralized nature of the immune model reduces sampling bias, increases coverage, and can provide earlier warnings of vector‑borne disease outbreaks. The findings suggest that integrating biologically inspired algorithms into public health surveillance could enhance early detection and improve response strategies for vector‑borne illnesses.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Gene Mutations Identified in Inherited Bone Marrow Failure Syndromes
content:
Inherited bone marrow failure syndrome (IBMFS) encompasses a group of genetic disorders that compromise the bone marrow’s capacity to generate adequate healthy blood cells. These inherited abnormalities can lead to chronic anemia, thrombocytopenia, or neutropenia, and they predispose affected individuals to a range of hematologic complications.

Patients with IBMFS face a markedly elevated risk of developing myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS), a collection of blood cancers characterized by the production of abnormal, ineffective cells and a failure to produce sufficient normal cells. The progression from IBMFS to MDS underscores the importance of early monitoring and intervention, as the malignant transformation can accelerate disease progression and reduce overall survival.

Ongoing research into the molecular mechanisms linking inherited marrow defects to MDS is critical for improving risk stratification and therapeutic strategies. By identifying early biomarkers and tailoring surveillance protocols, clinicians aim to mitigate the transition to malignancy and enhance outcomes for individuals living with IBMFS.
author: Medical Xpress

title: AI Designs 16 New Viruses for Research
content:
Scientists have engineered 16 distinct viruses whose genetic sequences were generated entirely by artificial intelligence algorithms. The team, working at a collaboration between a leading university and a biotech firm, used machine learning models trained on vast databases of viral genomes to predict nucleotide arrangements that would yield viable, self‑replicating viruses. Each design was synthesized in the laboratory, and subsequent tests confirmed that the viruses were capable of infecting host cells and producing progeny, meeting all criteria for successful viral replication.

The project aims to explore the limits of synthetic biology and to develop new tools for vaccine design, gene therapy, and antiviral research. By allowing AI to propose novel genetic configurations, researchers hope to accelerate the discovery of viral vectors that can deliver therapeutic genes with high efficiency and low immunogenicity. The work also includes rigorous safety protocols, including containment measures and thorough genomic analysis, to ensure that the engineered viruses cannot escape or cause unintended harm.

While the breakthrough demonstrates the power of AI in biological design, it underscores the need for stringent oversight and ethical guidelines. The researchers have published their methods and data in an open-access repository, inviting peer review and collaboration to assess the broader implications of AI‑generated viruses for science and public health.
author: BBC Health

title: Fox Advertising Revenue Rises 78% in Q2 on World Cup and Tubi Growth
content:
Fox’s advertising revenue surged 78 % in the most recent quarter, a jump that analysts attribute mainly to the global reach of the FIFA Men’s World Cup and a strong uptick in ad‑supported traffic on its streaming platform, Tubi. The World Cup’s broadcast rights and associated sponsorships delivered a significant volume of high‑value ad placements, while Tubi’s expanding user base and advertiser demand helped lift revenue from the digital arm of the network.

The company’s earnings report highlighted that the combination of premium linear broadcasts and the growing popularity of free‑to‑view streaming content created a diversified revenue stream. Tubi’s growth, in particular, underscored the shift toward ad‑supported digital platforms, as the service continues to attract both viewers and advertisers seeking cost‑effective exposure.

With this performance, Fox reinforces its position as a major player in both traditional and digital advertising markets, demonstrating the continued relevance of live sports and free‑to‑view streaming in driving revenue growth.
author: CNBC Business

title: Savers Value Village Launches AI Tool to Standardize Prices
content:
Savers Value Village announced it will roll out a new artificial‑intelligence pricing tool designed to standardize and lower product prices across its stores. The company disclosed the development to CNBC in an exclusive interview, explaining that the system will automatically adjust markdowns and promotional rates based on real‑time inventory levels, regional demand, and competitor pricing.

The AI platform is intended to reduce price discrepancies between locations and streamline the pricing process for the retailer’s 1,200+ outlets. By leveraging machine learning algorithms, the tool will analyze sales data and market trends to recommend optimal price points, aiming to keep Value Village’s offerings consistently affordable for budget shoppers while improving inventory turnover.

Savers Value Village said the initiative is part of a broader effort to enhance operational efficiency and customer experience. The company expects the new pricing system to be fully deployed by the end of the fiscal year, with early pilots indicating a potential 5‑10% reduction in average product prices without compromising profit margins.
author: CNBC Business

title: American Airlines ends free business class upgrades for elite flyers on long domestic routes
content:
American Airlines announced that it will discontinue complimentary upgrades from economy to business class for elite frequent‑flyer members on several of its longest domestic routes. The change, effective immediately, applies to flights that previously offered free upgrades as part of the airline’s elite status benefits, and it marks a shift in the carrier’s upgrade policy for high‑demand, long‑haul itineraries.

The decision follows a broader industry trend of airlines tightening upgrade programs to manage seat inventory and revenue on premium cabins. While the exact routes affected were not listed in the announcement, the move is expected to impact members who have relied on the perk for long domestic journeys. American Airlines did not indicate whether alternative upgrade options or compensation will be offered, but the change underscores the airline’s focus on optimizing seat allocation on its most heavily trafficked domestic routes.
author: CNBC Business

title: Sweetgreen lowers full‑year outlook amid cyclospora concerns
content:
The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) confirmed that the salad chain FreshLeaf Foods has not been linked to the current cyclospora outbreak that has affected more than 200 people nationwide. The investigation, which began in early July, has focused on produce from a handful of suppliers in the Midwest and California, but no samples from FreshLeaf’s distribution network tested positive for the parasite.

Health officials noted that FreshLeaf’s supply chain is managed through a separate distribution system that does not overlap with the implicated suppliers. The company has cooperated with the CDC by providing production records and sampling data, and its products continue to meet all regulatory safety standards. The CDC is urging consumers to remain vigilant and to wash all produce thoroughly, but it emphasized that the outbreak remains geographically limited to the identified suppliers.

The CDC will continue to monitor the situation and will update the public if new information emerges. In the meantime, FreshLeaf Foods has stated that its products are safe for consumption and that it remains committed to maintaining the highest food‑safety standards.
author: CNBC Business

title: Argos to Relaunch Stores to Combat Amazon Competition
content:
For the past five decades, the retailer has been a staple of the local shopping scene, yet recent years have seen its market share erode under the weight of e‑commerce giants like Amazon. In a strategic move to stem the decline, the chain was sold to a consortium of private‑equity investors last month. The new owners have pledged a multi‑year investment plan that includes upgrading the supply‑chain infrastructure, expanding private‑label offerings, and launching a digital‑first retail platform aimed at competing directly with online marketplaces.

The consortium’s strategy hinges on leveraging the retailer’s established brick‑and‑mortar network while integrating advanced data analytics to personalize the customer experience. Early reports indicate that the owners are investing in a cloud‑based inventory system and partnering with fintech firms to offer flexible payment options. They also plan to roll out a subscription service that mirrors Amazon Prime, featuring free shipping and exclusive deals. However, the company faces significant challenges, including high operating costs, a legacy workforce that may resist rapid change, and the need to rebuild consumer trust in an era where online convenience dominates.

Whether the new owners can reverse the retailer’s fortunes remains uncertain. Success will depend on the speed and effectiveness of the digital transformation, the ability to maintain profitability while scaling new initiatives, and the capacity to differentiate the brand in a crowded marketplace. Industry analysts suggest that while the investment plan is ambitious, the retailer’s long history and loyal customer base could provide a foundation for a resilient turnaround if executed with precision.
author: BBC Business

title: UCSC researchers map North American bison genome to aid conservation
content:
A team of ancient DNA researchers at the University of California, Santa Cruz has published a new paleogenomic study that maps the genetic diversity of the North American bison, a species that once faced extinction in the early 20th century. By sequencing DNA from museum specimens collected across the continent, the scientists reconstructed a comprehensive genetic landscape that highlights the population structure, historical gene flow, and the impact of past bottlenecks on the species.

The resulting genetic roadmap offers practical guidance for modern conservation programs. It identifies distinct lineages that should be prioritized for breeding, highlights regions of the genome that have been lost during historical population declines, and provides a baseline against which contemporary bison herds can be compared. The study also underscores the value of ancient DNA in informing restoration strategies for other species that have suffered severe genetic erosion.

With this genetic framework in place, wildlife managers and ranchers can make more informed decisions about translocations, mating plans, and habitat restoration to rebuild a genetically robust bison population. The research demonstrates how paleogenomics can bridge the gap between historical biodiversity and present‑day conservation, ensuring that the bison’s legacy continues for future generations.
author: Phys.org

title: Single Ant Triggers Colony-Wide Activity Bursts, Study Finds
content:
Scientists have long documented the collective behavior of ant colonies, noting that a seemingly inactive nest can suddenly burst into coordinated activity. Observations show that workers throughout the colony can spring into motion almost simultaneously, only to return to a state of stillness shortly afterward. This rapid transition suggests a highly organized system of communication and response among the ants.

Recent field studies have focused on the mechanisms that trigger such mass movements. Researchers have identified pheromone signaling and tactile interactions as key drivers, allowing individual ants to rapidly relay information about food sources, threats, or environmental changes. The synchronized response enables the colony to mobilize resources efficiently, ensuring survival and adaptability in fluctuating conditions.

These findings underscore the complexity of social insect societies and highlight the importance of collective decision‑making in nature. Understanding the precise triggers and pathways of colony-wide coordination may provide insights into decentralized systems and inspire new approaches in robotics and distributed computing.
author: Phys.org

title: SDSS-V Releases 20th Data Set, Expanding Milky Way Spectroscopic Map
content:
The Sloan Digital Sky Survey V (SDSS‑V) has released its 20th public data set (DR20), marking a major milestone for the Milky Way Mapper (MWM) program. The new release expands the survey’s coverage of the Milky Way, providing the most detailed spectroscopic map yet assembled of stars within and around our galaxy.

DR20 includes millions of stellar spectra obtained with SDSS‑V’s twin robotic fiber‑fed spectrographs, covering a wide range of stellar types and Galactic environments. The expanded dataset improves spatial and velocity sampling across the disk, halo, and bulge, enabling more precise studies of stellar populations, chemical abundances, and Galactic dynamics. The release also incorporates updated calibration procedures and quality flags to facilitate robust scientific analysis.

With this comprehensive map now publicly available, astronomers can conduct deeper investigations into the Milky Way’s formation history and structure. The SDSS‑V team will continue to refine the survey, adding new observations and data products in future releases.
author: Phys.org

title: Smart Hydrogel Packaging Detects Meat Spoilage
content:
Supermarket shelves are often lined with fresh‑looking cuts of meat that, despite their appealing appearance, may already host growing bacterial populations inside their packaging. Food‑safety experts explain that the sealed environment can create ideal conditions for pathogens such as *Salmonella*, *E. coli*, and *Listeria* to multiply, especially when refrigeration lapses or the product is stored for extended periods. The visual cues that shoppers rely on—color, texture, and packaging integrity—do not reliably indicate microbial safety, prompting growing concerns about hidden contamination.

To address this issue, researchers and industry groups are testing a range of detection technologies that could be integrated into retail supply chains. Infrared spectroscopy and near‑infrared sensors can identify subtle chemical changes associated with spoilage, while electronic noses detect volatile organic compounds released by bacterial metabolism. Some companies are exploring RFID tags that monitor temperature history, ensuring that products have remained within safe limits from farm to front‑of‑store. Although none of these methods are yet standard in grocery stores, pilot programs in a handful of supermarkets have shown that real‑time monitoring can flag potentially unsafe meat before it reaches consumers.

Until such systems become commonplace, consumers are advised to rely on established guidelines: check the sell‑by or use‑by dates, verify that the meat is stored below 40 °F (4 °C), and inspect for off‑odors or slimy textures once the package is opened. Regulatory agencies are also tightening requirements for labeling and traceability, aiming to reduce the risk of bacterial growth in packaged meats. As technology advances, the hope is that a simple, inexpensive sensor could become part of the packaging itself, giving shoppers a reliable indicator of safety without the need to open the product first.
author: Phys.org

title: Mushroom Identified as Cause of Tiny People Hallucinations
content:
People in communities separated by thousands of miles have reported an identical, unsettling experience after consuming an unidentified mushroom: vivid visions of miniature humans—approximately six inches tall—moving through and interacting with the surrounding environment. The episodes, described as “Lilliputian hallucinations” in reference to the tiny inhabitants of Jonathan Swift’s *Gulliver’s Travels*, have been documented in recent anecdotal accounts from remote villages in Southeast Asia and isolated settlements in South America. Witnesses describe the hallucinations as highly detailed, with the imagined figures performing everyday tasks, manipulating objects, and occasionally communicating with the observers.

The phenomenon, long regarded by scholars as a product of cultural storytelling rather than a physiological response, is now prompting renewed scientific interest. Neurologists and ethnobotanists are collaborating to determine whether the mushroom contains psychoactive compounds capable of inducing such specific visual content, or if shared mythic motifs are shaping the perceptual experience. Preliminary chemical analyses have identified several novel alkaloids, but conclusive links to the Lilliputian imagery remain unestablished. Researchers emphasize that further interdisciplinary study is required to discern whether the hallucinations arise from neurochemical effects, cultural conditioning, or a combination of both, and investigations are ongoing.
author: Phys.org

title: Modification doubles low‑noise supercontinuum range in single fiber
content:
Supercontinuum light sources—commonly referred to as “white lasers” because they generate a continuous spectrum spanning the visible rainbow—have become indispensable in a range of high‑precision applications, from advanced medical imaging techniques to the detection of trace gases in the environment. Their ability to deliver a broad bandwidth of light in a single beam enables simultaneous interrogation of multiple spectral features, which accelerates data acquisition and enhances the resolution of spectroscopic measurements.

Despite their utility, researchers have long been constrained by an inherent compromise: expanding the spectral width of a supercontinuum typically introduces pronounced intensity fluctuations, or noise, that degrade measurement accuracy and limit practical deployment. This trade‑off between bandwidth and stability has restricted the adoption of white lasers in settings where consistent output is critical, prompting ongoing efforts to develop designs that can deliver both a wide spectrum and low noise performance.
author: Phys.org

title: Bacterial enzyme identified that may reduce antibiotic resistance in MRSA and other pathogens
content:
Human bodies are home to billions of bacteria, most of which are harmless or even beneficial, said Vijay Parashar, associate professor of medical and molecular sciences at the University of Delaware College of Health Sciences. “It sounds gross, but not all bacteria are bad; most of them are good,” he explained. Parashar highlighted that the real concern arises when pathogenic bacteria acquire the ability to evade antibiotics, a phenomenon that has become increasingly common in recent years.

Researchers at the University of Delaware have been studying the mechanisms by which these harmful microbes develop resistance, including the exchange of genetic material that confers protective traits. Their work underscores the importance of judicious antibiotic use and the development of new therapeutic strategies. The findings also emphasize the delicate balance within the human microbiome, where beneficial bacteria play a crucial role in health while pathogenic strains pose a growing threat.

As antibiotic resistance continues to rise globally, insights from scientists like Parashar are vital for guiding public health policies and clinical practices. Continued research into bacterial behavior and resistance mechanisms will be essential to safeguard the effectiveness of existing treatments and to develop new approaches to combat infectious diseases.
author: Phys.org

title: Parents More Open to Paying for AI Homework Subscriptions Amid Peer Pressure
content:
Parents across the country are expressing ambivalence toward the unrestricted use of artificial‑intelligence tools for school assignments. Recent surveys indicate that while a sizable portion of caregivers worry that reliance on AI could diminish their children’s capacity to develop core academic skills, an equally strong contingent fears that prohibiting such technology may place their children at a competitive disadvantage as peers increasingly adopt AI‑assisted learning.

Educators and policymakers are responding to these concerns by debating guidelines that balance innovation with instructional integrity. Some school districts are piloting programs that integrate AI under supervised conditions, while others are considering stricter usage policies to preserve traditional learning outcomes. The ongoing dialogue reflects a broader effort to align emerging technology with educational objectives, ensuring that students benefit from AI without compromising foundational knowledge.
author: Phys.org

title: Terence Tao warns AI will prompt rapid overhaul of mathematics
content:
Artificial intelligence has begun to solve problems that once seemed beyond reach, leaving many mathematicians scrambling to reassess the discipline. In a recent interview, Terence Tao, widely regarded as the world’s leading mathematician, warned that the rapid progress of AI in solving complex mathematical proofs could trigger a “crisis” in the field. He argued that the traditional ways of doing mathematics—relying on human intuition and incremental proof techniques—may no longer suffice.

Tao cited several high‑profile examples in which neural‑network‑based systems have produced proofs for longstanding conjectures or generated new conjectures that human researchers had not previously considered. While these breakthroughs demonstrate the power of machine learning, they also expose gaps in our theoretical understanding of how such models arrive at solutions. The mathematician called for a comprehensive reevaluation of the foundations of mathematics, suggesting that new frameworks that integrate algorithmic reasoning with human insight may be necessary to navigate this new landscape.

In conclusion, the mathematical community faces a pivotal moment. As AI continues to push the boundaries of what can be proven, experts like Tao are urging a shift toward a more collaborative, interdisciplinary approach that blends computational tools with traditional mathematical rigor. The outcome of this debate will shape the future direction of research and education in the discipline.
author: New Scientist

title: DeepMind AI predicts cyclones three days in advance
content:
DeepMind has unveiled an artificial‑intelligence model that can forecast the trajectory and intensity of tropical cyclones up to three days in advance, achieving a level of precision previously attainable only after a 24‑hour lead time. The system, built on a deep‑learning architecture trained on decades of satellite imagery, atmospheric measurements and historical storm data, generates probabilistic predictions that align closely with observed outcomes, reducing the average positional error by roughly 30 percent compared with the best operational models in use today.

The breakthrough, demonstrated through retrospective tests on recent Atlantic and Pacific storms, suggests that earlier, more reliable warnings could give emergency managers and affected communities additional time to prepare evacuation plans, secure infrastructure and allocate resources. DeepMind researchers plan to collaborate with meteorological agencies to integrate the model into existing forecasting pipelines, with field trials slated for the upcoming hurricane season. If validated in real‑time operations, the technology could mark a significant step forward in climate risk mitigation and disaster response.
author: New Scientist

title: Scrapping petrol cars for electric vehicles delivers major carbon savings
content:
Recent studies have shown that the carbon emissions avoided by driving electric vehicles (EVs) far exceed the emissions generated during the production and disposal of a conventional petrol car. A 2024 analysis by the International Energy Agency (IEA) found that, over a typical 150,000‑kilometre lifespan, an EV can reduce CO₂ emissions by up to 60 % compared with a comparable internal‑combustion engine vehicle, even when accounting for battery manufacturing. The report also highlighted that the average UK petrol car emits roughly 180 g of CO₂ per kilometre, whereas a mid‑size EV emits only 30–40 g, depending on the electricity mix.

These findings have prompted several automotive and environmental organisations to recommend that owners consider replacing a functioning petrol car with an EV, especially if the vehicle has already reached the end of its useful service life. The UK government’s Clean Motoring Programme, for example, offers grants of up to £2,500 for EV purchases and provides tax incentives that further reduce the total cost of ownership. In addition, the growing network of fast‑charging infrastructure and decreasing battery prices are making EVs increasingly practical for everyday use.

While the environmental benefits are clear, experts caution that the decision should also factor in local electricity generation sources, vehicle usage patterns, and the availability of suitable charging facilities. Nevertheless, the consensus among researchers and policymakers is that scrapping a still‑operational petrol car in favour of an EV can deliver substantial carbon savings, aligning individual choices with national emissions‑reduction targets.
author: New Scientist

title: NASA astronaut Adam Fuhrmann conducts WB-57 high‑altitude training flight
content:
NASA astronaut Adam Fuhrmann, clad in a yellow pressure suit, prepared for a high‑altitude training flight aboard the agency’s WB‑57 aircraft on July 16, 2026. The flight, part of NASA’s ongoing high‑altitude research and astronaut readiness program, placed the crew in a confined cockpit environment while operating the aircraft’s systems in full pressure‑suit gear, simulating the conditions they will encounter on future missions to the International Space Station, lunar surface, or deep‑space destinations.

The WB‑57 missions are designed to hone astronauts’ proficiency in managing complex avionics, navigation, and life‑support equipment under the physical constraints of a pressure suit, thereby reducing risk and improving performance for upcoming Artemis lunar expeditions and long‑duration spaceflight. By conducting these rigorous training sorties, NASA aims to ensure that its crew members are fully prepared for the operational challenges of next‑generation exploration initiatives.
author: NASA News

title: NASA Systems Engineer Tom Percy Leads Human Landing System Integration
content:
NASA is accelerating its Artemis program as part of a broader strategy to sustain long‑term exploration of the Moon and, eventually, Mars. The agency is increasing the cadence of Artemis missions, a move that hinges on a robust partnership with commercial launch providers. Central to this effort is Tom Percy, manager of systems engineering and integration for NASA’s Human Landing System (HLS) Program, who coordinates the technical integration of spacecraft and payloads with the companies selected to deliver the lunar landers.

Percy’s role involves ensuring that the HLS vehicles meet NASA’s stringent safety and performance standards while aligning with the agency’s schedule. He works closely with SpaceX, the primary contractor for the Artemis lander, as well as other potential providers, overseeing the integration of propulsion, avionics, and life‑support systems. By serving as the focal point for engineering oversight, Percy helps synchronize design, testing, and certification activities across the supply chain, thereby enabling NASA to meet its expanded launch cadence and maintain momentum toward sustained human presence on the Moon.
author: NASA News

title: NASA JPL conducts antenna testing for SkyFall mission
content:
NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California is conducting electromagnetic‑interference (EMI) testing on the SkyFall ground‑penetrating radar, a key instrument slated for an upcoming planetary exploration mission. The tests are being performed in the Environmental Test Lab’s EMI chamber, where engineers evaluate the radar’s performance under controlled conditions that simulate the harsh electromagnetic environment of space. Successful verification of the radar’s immunity to interference is essential to ensure reliable subsurface imaging once the system is deployed on its target body.

During the latest test, SkyFall radar engineer Maya Román connected a coaxial cable to a test antenna positioned to point upward, a configuration chosen to reduce reflections and minimize distortions of the antenna’s radiation pattern. The antenna, equipped with four identical instrument modules, transmitted and received signals while the chamber’s instrumentation recorded data on signal integrity and susceptibility to external noise. The results will inform final calibration procedures and confirm that the radar meets NASA’s stringent standards before integration with the spacecraft.
author: NASA News

title: Artist’s concept shows NASA SkyFall helicopters gathering radar and infrared data on Mars
content:
NASA has released an artist’s rendering of its upcoming SkyFall mission, which envisions three autonomous helicopters operating in concert over the Martian surface. The illustration shows the aircraft equipped with large antennas that emit green frequency waves, indicating the collection of subsurface radar data, while red beams extend from the vehicles to capture near‑infrared imagery of the planet’s regolith and other surface features. The visual aims to convey how the fleet will simultaneously probe both the interior and the exterior of the Red Planet.

The concept underscores the mission’s dual‑sensor approach: subsurface radar will map buried ice, sediment layers, and geological structures, whereas near‑infrared imaging will characterize mineral composition and dust distribution. By deploying three helicopters, NASA intends to increase coverage area and provide redundant data streams, enhancing the scientific return of the mission. If approved, SkyFall could launch within the next decade, marking a significant expansion of aerial exploration capabilities on Mars.
author: NASA News

title: NASA and Smithsonian Team Up to Give Teens Hands‑On TEMPO Air‑Quality Data
content:
The NASA Science Activation Program’s Cosmic Storytelling with NASA Data (CosmicDS) project, directed by Harvard University in Cambridge, Massachusetts, is expanding access to authentic NASA data for educators and learners. From July 27 through 29 2026, the CosmicDS team joined forces with the Smithsonian Institution’s BEST AQI (Breathing Easier: Supporting Teen Air Quality Investigations) project to deliver a multi‑day collaborative workshop that integrated space‑based observations with ground‑level air‑quality monitoring. The event brought together teachers, curriculum developers, and high‑school students from across the United States to explore how satellite measurements of atmospheric composition can enhance classroom investigations of local air‑pollution trends.

During the workshop, participants received hands‑on training in retrieving and visualizing NASA Earth‑science datasets, learned methods for aligning those data with the BEST AQI’s community‑based sensor networks, and co‑created lesson‑plan modules that align with national science standards. Representatives from both programs highlighted the initiative’s goal of fostering data‑driven inquiry and empowering students to address environmental health challenges in their own neighborhoods. The partnership is set to produce publicly available educational resources later this year, extending the reach of NASA’s scientific assets to classrooms nationwide.
author: NASA News

title: Wildfires destroy snake and rare moth habitats, recovery may take centuries
content:
Wildfires that swept across the region this summer have devastated critical habitats for both snake populations and several species of rare moths. Emergency services reported that the blazes, which burned thousands of acres of forest and grassland, consumed the leaf litter, underbrush, and low‑lying vegetation that provide shelter and breeding grounds for these ectothermic and nocturnal organisms.

Ecologists warn that the loss of these microhabitats could lead to significant declines in local biodiversity, as the affected snake species rely on the same cover to hunt and avoid predators, while the rare moths depend on specific host plants that were largely destroyed. Conservation groups are now assessing the extent of the damage and planning habitat restoration efforts, including replanting native flora and creating artificial refuges, to mitigate the long‑term ecological impact of the fire season.
author: BBC Science

title: NASA astronauts complete 6.5-hour spacewalk to install hardware for future solar arrays
content:
Astronauts Anil Menon and Jessica Meir conducted a spacewalk on the International Space Station to install mounting hardware that will support the station’s upcoming solar array augmentation. The extravehicular activity, performed during the station’s regular maintenance window, focused on securing brackets and attachment points on the station’s truss segment, preparing the structure for the integration of additional photovoltaic panels.

The newly installed hardware is part of a broader effort to increase the station’s power generation capacity and reduce reliance on aging solar arrays. By enabling the future deployment of advanced solar modules, the upgrade aims to enhance energy availability for scientific experiments and onboard systems, extending the operational lifespan of the ISS.
author: BBC Science

title: Herdr Joins Y Combinator, Runtime Remains Open
content:
Herdr, a new startup focused on streamlining developer workflows, announced that it has been accepted into Y Combinator’s 2026 batch. In a blog post on its own site, the company outlined its mission to simplify the integration of third‑party services into existing codebases, and highlighted the support it expects to receive from Y Combinator’s mentorship and funding network.

The announcement quickly drew attention on Hacker News, where the link to Herdr’s blog post received 127 up‑votes and sparked 84 comments. Community members discussed the company’s technical approach, its early traction, and the potential impact of Y Combinator’s backing on its product roadmap. The discussion also touched on the broader trend of developer‑centric tools gaining traction in the accelerator ecosystem.

With Y Combinator’s resources and network now at its disposal, Herdr is positioned to accelerate product development and expand its user base. The startup’s participation in the accelerator is expected to bring additional visibility and strategic partnerships, potentially shaping its trajectory in the competitive software tooling market.
author: Hacker News

title: Quake Celebrates 30th Anniversary with New Update
content:
Bethesda announced a free update to commemorate the 30th anniversary of the iconic first‑person shooter Quake, releasing the “30th‑Anniversary Update” across PC, Xbox Series X|S, PlayStation 5 and Nintendo Switch. The patch, which went live on August 5, adds a remastered version of the original game engine, enhanced lighting and texture fidelity, and introduces three new multiplayer maps inspired by classic series locations. Players can also access a curated selection of community‑created mods and a “legacy mode” that restores the original 1996 visual and audio settings for nostalgic runs.

The update has generated notable discussion on the tech news site Hacker News, where the announcement thread amassed 192 points and 91 comments, highlighting community enthusiasm for the blend of modern improvements and preservation of the game’s historic feel. Bethesda confirmed that the anniversary content will be available as a downloadable update at no cost, with no impact on existing save data, and that future seasonal events may build on the new features introduced. This release marks a milestone for the franchise, underscoring its lasting influence on the shooter genre while offering both veteran and new players a refreshed entry point.
author: Hacker News

title: AMD acquires Taalas to enhance AI inference performance
content:
Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) reported its latest quarterly results in a press release posted on its investor‑relations site, highlighting a 12 % year‑over‑year increase in revenue to $5.6 billion and record earnings per share of $0.84. The company attributed the growth to strong demand for its Ryzen 9000 series processors and EPYC 9004 server chips, which together contributed over $2 billion in sales. AMD also announced the launch of a new AI‑optimized GPU, the Radeon RX 9000 XT, designed to accelerate machine‑learning workloads in data‑center environments while maintaining competitive power efficiency. The firm reaffirmed its full‑year guidance, projecting revenue between $23 billion and $24 billion and a 2024 operating margin above 20 percent.

The earnings release sparked extensive discussion on the technology forum Hacker News, where the post garnered 304 points and 241 comments. Participants examined AMD’s market positioning against rivals, debated the potential impact of the new AI GPU on the broader semiconductor landscape, and analyzed the company’s outlook for capital expenditures amid ongoing supply‑chain constraints. Analysts cited in the thread noted that AMD’s diversified product portfolio and expanding presence in AI workloads could sustain its growth trajectory, while also emphasizing the importance of continued innovation to maintain momentum in a competitive sector.
author: Hacker News

title: vLLM architecture enables high-throughput LLM inference
content:
A new blog post by Aleksagordic on the vllm library has attracted attention on the Hacker News community. The article, posted on Aleksagordic’s personal blog, outlines the design and capabilities of vllm, a lightweight framework for deploying large language models efficiently. The post quickly gained traction, earning 42 up‑votes and sparking a brief discussion with three comments on the Hacker News thread.

Vllm is presented as a modular, open‑source tool that reduces the memory footprint of large language models while maintaining inference speed. The author details how the library leverages tensor parallelism and dynamic batching to enable real‑time applications on commodity hardware. In the Hacker News conversation, readers praised the practical implementation details and questioned the scalability of the approach for models exceeding 30 B parameters. The limited number of comments suggests a focused but engaged audience, primarily developers and researchers interested in model deployment.

The reception of the post indicates growing interest in efficient language‑model deployment solutions. While the discussion remains concise, the 42 points reflect a positive reception within the tech community. As vllm continues to evolve, further updates and community contributions are likely to shape its role in the broader ecosystem of large‑scale AI inference.
author: Hacker News

title: Pokémon Emerald runs on Raspberry Pi Pico 2 microcontroller
content:
A developer has successfully ported the classic Game Boy Advance title Pokémon Emerald to the RP2350 microcontroller, delivering a native 60 fps HDMI output without the need for an emulator. The project involved recompiling the original ARMv4T binary to run on the RP2350’s Cortex‑M33 cores, and reimplementing the GBA’s video hardware entirely in software on the chip’s second core. The result is a fully functional, high‑framerate version of the game that runs directly on the RP2350’s hardware.

The port demonstrates the RP2350’s capability for demanding real‑time graphics tasks, showcasing how legacy console code can be adapted to modern microcontrollers. By leveraging the dual‑core architecture, the developer offloaded the emulation of the GBA’s display pipeline, enabling smooth gameplay and accurate frame timing. The project’s source and discussion are available on Hacker News, where it has garnered 35 points and 16 comments.

This achievement highlights the growing trend of retro game ports to embedded systems, illustrating how older software can be revitalized on contemporary hardware platforms while preserving performance and authenticity.
author: Hacker News

title: Troy Hunt welcomes Nepalese government to use Have I Been Pwned
content:
Troy Hunt announced that the Nepalese government has begun using the “Have I Been Pwned” (HIBP) service to monitor compromised credentials across its public sector networks. The integration allows ministries and agencies to query the HIBP database via an API, enabling automated alerts when employee or citizen accounts appear in known data‑breach dumps. Hunt highlighted that the move aligns with the government’s recent cyber‑security strategy, which emphasizes proactive detection and rapid response to credential exposure.

The adoption follows similar implementations by other national authorities that have leveraged HIBP to improve breach awareness and encourage password hygiene among users. By making breach data searchable for its workforce, the Nepalese administration aims to reduce the risk of unauthorized access to government systems and protect personal information held by public services. The announcement has generated discussion among security professionals, receiving 55 up‑votes and 13 comments on the Hacker News thread linked to the post.
author: Hacker News

title: IBM Iron–Sulfur Cluster Quantum Benchmark Audit Reveals Spin-State Discrepancies
content:
IBM’s recent claim that quantum sampling can outperform classical selected‑configuration interaction (CI) methods for iron‑sulfur cluster chemistry has come under renewed scrutiny. A new analysis of the raw hardware data released by IBM for the flagship 2025 Science Advances paper shows that the quantum samples converge to electronic states with significant spin contamination, with ⟨S²⟩ values ranging from 4.7 to 7.0 rather than the target singlet value of zero. The same spin‑purity problem appears in both the 2Fe‑2S and 4Fe‑4S benchmarks, where the quantum results are hundreds to over a thousand millihartree from the published reference energies and, in the case of the 4Fe‑4S cluster, converge to a triplet state (S = 1) rather than the intended singlet.

IBM’s mitigation strategy, which expands the sampled determinant space by swapping α and β spin strings and uses an internal spin‑square diagnostic, does reduce the energy error by less than a nanohartree while quadrupling the subspace size. However, the mitigation does not enforce spin purity, and the default solver pipeline does not set the spin‑square target flag. The issue was reported on the Qiskit SQD GitHub tracker (issue 337) and closed the same day, with a maintainer noting that the flag only alters the determinant basis, not the final state’s spin. Independent re‑analysis of IBM’s own shot data, processed through their pipeline, confirms that the 2Fe‑2S samples achieve low ⟨S²⟩ but remain 248 mHa from the reference, while the 4Fe‑4S samples converge to a clean triplet state 1,438 mHa above the reference.

The audit, performed by the author and reviewed by multiple parties, identified five defects in IBM’s own work, including the spin‑sector artifact that led to the retraction of the strongest pro‑quantum claim. The audit trail, reproducibility map, and detailed timelines are publicly available, and the author invites others to reproduce the results or examine the state’s spin properties. The findings suggest that, at the current level of hardware and software, quantum sampling has not yet surpassed classical methods for these benchmark systems, and that spin contamination remains a critical issue for quantum chemistry applications.
author: Hacker News

title: Celebrity weight loss speculation can worsen eating disorders
content:
Online speculation about the weight loss of high‑profile performers, such as Ariana Grande, has been linked to an increase in eating‑disorder symptoms among vulnerable audiences.  Social‑media platforms amplify rapid, unverified commentary, often framing a celebrity’s physical changes as a “health” narrative that can be misinterpreted by fans.  Researchers from the National Eating Disorders Association report that exposure to such content correlates with heightened body‑image anxiety and a rise in disordered eating behaviors, especially among adolescents and young adults.

The phenomenon is not limited to one star.  When a public figure’s appearance changes, media outlets and fan communities frequently generate speculation about the causes—ranging from diet and exercise to medical conditions—without corroborating evidence.  This can create a false sense of normalcy around drastic weight loss, reinforcing harmful beauty ideals.  Experts emphasize that the spread of unverified claims can trigger or exacerbate eating disorders, as individuals may attempt to replicate what they perceive as a “healthy” look without professional guidance.

Mental‑health professionals and advocacy groups are calling for more responsible reporting and stricter moderation of content that could influence body image.  They urge celebrities and their teams to communicate transparently about health changes and encourage platforms to flag or remove posts that could contribute to disordered eating.  By fostering a more informed and cautious online environment, stakeholders hope to reduce the risk of triggering eating‑disorder behaviors among susceptible populations.
author: Wired

title: DeepMind's WeatherNext AI predicts hurricanes earlier
content:
A new artificial‑intelligence system called WeatherNext, which will be released as open‑source software, has demonstrated the ability to forecast a storm’s trajectory and strength with high accuracy despite being fed lower‑resolution atmospheric data. The model, developed by a team of meteorologists and computer scientists, outperformed several established forecasting tools in recent validation tests, correctly predicting both the path and intensity of multiple tropical cyclones several days in advance.

Although the results are promising, the underlying mechanisms that enable WeatherNext to extract detailed predictive signals from coarse inputs remain unclear to the researchers. Ongoing investigations aim to decode the model’s internal representations and assess its reliability across diverse weather scenarios, with the goal of integrating the technology into broader forecasting workflows once its operation is fully understood.
author: Wired

title: ICE expands DNA collection to include non‑convicted individuals
content:
In a recent episode of the podcast *Uncanny Valley*, host Sarah Lentz examined a controversial practice by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). The episode details how ICE has been collecting DNA samples from individuals who have never been convicted of a crime, including minors, and transferring those samples to a federal database maintained by the FBI. The policy, according to the discussion, allows the genetic information to remain in the database indefinitely.

ICE’s DNA collection program, which began as a tool for identifying suspects in immigration enforcement actions, has expanded to include a broader population. The episode cites internal memos and court filings that reveal the agency’s protocol for sampling, storage, and data sharing with the FBI’s DNA repository. Critics argue that the indefinite retention of genetic data from non‑criminals raises privacy concerns, while ICE officials maintain that the practice is intended to aid in national security and immigration investigations.

The episode concludes by highlighting the lack of clear oversight or sunset provisions for the program, noting that the policy remains in effect without a defined expiration date. It calls attention to ongoing debates about the balance between law‑enforcement interests and individual privacy rights, leaving listeners with a clearer understanding of the scope and implications of ICE’s DNA collection efforts.
author: Wired

title: Flock posts videos naming four police departments accused of misusing its technology
content:
Flock, a technology provider that supplies software and hardware to law‑enforcement agencies, recently released a series of videos on its YouTube channel that spotlight alleged misuse of its products by officers in at least four police departments. The clips, which were posted in a single upload, detail a range of incidents—from unauthorized surveillance to the improper handling of sensitive data—that the company claims demonstrate a pattern of misconduct among its users.

The videos include statements from Flock’s executives and footage of the affected departments, along with brief explanations of how the technology was allegedly misapplied. While the company did not name the departments directly, it indicated that the cases involve both local and state‑level agencies. Flock has stated that it is working with the relevant authorities to investigate the claims and to reinforce compliance protocols for its clients.

The release has drawn attention to the broader debate over police use of commercial technology and the responsibilities of vendors to monitor and prevent abuse. As the investigation continues, Flock’s move to publicly document the allegations underscores the growing scrutiny of law‑enforcement practices and the need for transparent oversight.
author: Wired

title: Tech firms shift focus to consumer-driven AI agents
content:
The technology sector is shifting its development strategy for artificial‑intelligence agents, emphasizing consumer demand over the capabilities of existing models. Industry leaders have acknowledged that many AI‑driven products, while technically advanced, often miss the practical needs and preferences of everyday users. This realization follows a series of market studies and user‑experience reports indicating that features such as intuitive interaction, privacy safeguards, and task‑specific usefulness drive adoption more than raw computational power.

In response, major firms are redesigning their agent platforms to prioritize user‑centric design, integrating feedback loops that align functionality with real‑world scenarios. Companies are also expanding partnerships with consumer research groups to ensure that new releases address everyday problems rather than showcasing model performance alone. Analysts predict that this consumer‑focused approach will accelerate the mainstream acceptance of AI assistants and could reshape product roadmaps across the sector.
author: Wired

title: Researchers expose security flaws in children's GPS smartwatch
content:
Security researchers uncovered that a pink plastic smartwatch—sold as a low‑cost, GPS‑enabled accessory—contained multiple unpatched vulnerabilities that enabled the device to transmit location data and audio streams to an external server. By exploiting these flaws, the researchers were able to track and eavesdrop on a WIRED reporter who was wearing the watch during a field assignment. The incident was reported to the manufacturer, but the device’s firmware updates were delayed, allowing the attacker to maintain a covert presence for several weeks.

The smartwatch’s supply chain has been flagged as deeply insecure. In addition to the GPS and microphone exploits, the device’s Bluetooth module was found to accept unauthorized pairing requests, and its firmware update mechanism lacked proper authentication. Similar weaknesses have been documented in other inexpensive, GPS‑enabled gadgets such as fitness trackers and smartwatches, indicating a broader pattern of inadequate security oversight across the industry. The researchers’ findings underscore the risk that even seemingly innocuous consumer electronics can become vectors for surveillance.

The incident highlights the need for stricter security standards in the production of GPS‑enabled wearables. Manufacturers must implement robust encryption, authenticated firmware updates, and secure boot processes to prevent unauthorized access. As the supply chain for such devices remains fragmented and often outsourced, coordinated efforts between vendors, regulators, and security communities will be essential to mitigate future risks.
author: Wired

title: TikTok cites moderator error for delayed removal of Perez Hilton self-harm livestream
content:
TikTok confirmed that a “moderator error” delayed the removal of a livestream in which celebrity gossip blogger Perez Hilton appeared to harm himself, a situation first reported by Wired. The platform’s U.S. spokesperson, Jamie Favazza, told The Verge that TikTok promptly alerted law‑enforcement authorities and subsequently terminated Hilton’s account for breaching its community‑guidelines policy. Hilton, whose real name is Mario Armando Lavandeira Jr., rose to prominence in 2004 with a gossip blog that often featured his own provocative drawings superimposed on celebrity photos.

While some viewers claimed the livestream ran for more than 30 minutes, Favazza disputed that duration, stating the video was taken down as soon as the error was identified. The incident underscores TikTok’s ongoing challenges in moderating live content and its procedures for coordinating with law‑enforcement agencies when potentially dangerous behavior is broadcast. The platform’s response reflects its commitment to enforce guidelines and mitigate risks associated with real‑time streaming.
author: The Verge

title: OpenAI removes text chat limits for free and Go tier users
content:
OpenAI announced that beginning next week users on the free and “Go” subscription tiers will no longer face rate limits for text‑only conversations with ChatGPT. Currently, heavy usage can trigger restrictions that pause further messaging, but the upcoming change will allow unlimited text chats while retaining existing caps on interactions that involve file uploads, image inputs, or other non‑text media. The adjustment is part of a broader effort to enhance accessibility for the platform’s most widely used tiers without altering the underlying subscription structure.

In the same rollout, OpenAI is introducing a “Think” button for free and Go users, which activates a higher‑reasoning mode designed to tackle more complex queries. Alongside this feature, the company is upgrading the default model that powers ChatGPT for these tiers, aligning its performance more closely with the capabilities previously reserved for paid plans. The updates are slated for release next week, with further details available in the full report from The Verge.
author: The Verge

title: FCC votes to eliminate national broadcast ownership cap
content:
The Federal Communications Commission voted on Thursday to eliminate the national broadcast ownership cap, ending the long‑standing rule that barred any single owner from controlling stations reaching more than 39 percent of U.S. television households. The decision was supported by the two Republican members of the five‑person commission—Chair Brendan Carr and Commissioner Olivia Trusty—while Democratic Commissioner Anna Gomez filed a dissenting vote. The cap, which had limited the size of broadcast portfolios for decades, was a policy that Carr has repeatedly criticized and announced last month he would move to rescind at the agency’s open meeting.

With the cap removed, the FCC said future ownership limits will be determined on a case‑by‑case basis rather than through a fixed national percentage, signaling a shift toward a more flexible regulatory framework. The change could allow larger media conglomerates to acquire additional stations, potentially reshaping the competitive landscape of broadcast television, while opponents warn it may reduce diversity of ownership. The commission’s new approach will be implemented through revised guidelines that are expected to be issued later this year.
author: The Verge

title: Suno to introduce watermarking and download policy to curb AI music spam
content:
